summary:
Orbital Forge is a browser based Space Mission Design Game in which you design and fly a complete space mission. You choose your science objective, your spacecraft bus, your scientific instruments, your orbit and your launch vehicle, all whilst managing the constraints of budget, mass, power, data and lifetime.
It deals with the problem by turning the abstract systems engineering trade-offs into actual decisions. Every choice has its consequences: a very capable instrument will give you a lot of science return but at the cost of mass, power, cost and the data that you have to downlink. You have a built-in launch vehicle check, a live resource dashboard and you get random events (e.g. a micrometeoroid hit) to mirror the real world constraints. You get a post-flight report which scores eight categories and explains each of those in plain English, and links the design choices back to real NASA missions (Landsat, Hubble etc).
This is important because the current tools out there teach the space concepts in isolation. There's a gap between the individual topics and the actual decision making in a mission. Orbital Forge closes that gap. It's accessible to the novice via tooltips and 3 difficulty levels, it's collaborative for up to 4 people in a team with different engineering roles and it's all based on NASA's systems engineering approach (GMAT) and JPL's CML. You learn why a mission works or doesn't work rather than just whether it does or not.
details:
Orbital Forge is a browser-based space mission design game (all in one HTML/CSS/JS file). You build your entire mission in six stages: science objective, spacecraft bus, instruments, orbit, launch vehicle, and launch. There's a live dashboard that tracks your budget, mass, power, and data as you go, and at the end of the mission you get a post-flight report that scores your mission across eight categories, explaining each point in plain English and linking your design to real NASA missions.

The game really does make the systems engineering trade-offs tangible (better instruments = more science return but also more mass, more power, more cost, and more data that you've got to downlink). There are three difficulty levels, random events (e.g., micrometeoroid hits), and team play for up to 4 players, with each player having a different role.

Its impact is in closing the gap between learning about individual space concepts and then being able to make integrated mission decisions. It's accessible to the novice through embedded explanations, and failure is a learning opportunity. It's built on NASA's systems engineering approach (GMAT) and JPL's CML
